*Losses In Bond Portfolios Seen As Potential Trigger To Further Selloff, CIO Says
*Mortgage-Backed Securities Look Attractive As Yields Rise, CIO Says
Investors Shouldn't Rush Into Bonds, Despite Rising Yields — Interview
By Paulo Trevisani

U.S. Treasury yields look attractive after September's sharp increase but they need to stabilize to attract more buyers, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes.

The 10-year benchmark yield rose more than half of a percent this month, its largest monthly increase in two years. The 30-year rose even faster, as markets worried about the U.S. economic outlook in face of rising government spending, inflation and increasing demand for credit to finance AI buildup.

For many investors, locking in the fat yields for the long run in one of the safest assets in the world could be a no-brainer. But active bonds portfolio managers also need to consider bond prices, which fall when yields rise. For them, the risk of Treasuries getting even cheaper could be a deterrent.

Individual investors "have the opportunity to reallocate out of equities, which have done incredibly well over the last three to five years, and into fixed income in some of the highest nominal and real yields that we've seen in over a generation," he said.
Gallo's portfolio at Federated Hermes, a firm managing $912 billion in assets, focuses on the total return of a bond over the next few years, so he isn't jumping in just yet.
"I'm still a little cautious in the face of the elevated interest rate volatility," he said.
Gallo worries that investors who increased their fixed-income bets in past years might get disappointed with the price performance and dump their bonds.

"I wonder if...the recent losses posted on a diversified bond portfolio motivate some individual investors to pull out of their bond funds, bringing a wave of redemptions that could cause [a] last blow-off of price weakness with yields rising a little bit further from here."
Bond yields have been unusually volatile in recent weeks. Treasury yields remain near multidecade highs after briefly falling on milder-than-expected August inflation data on Wednesday.

Yields have been rising as the inflationary pressures brought by the Middle East conflict drastically changed the economic outlook. Earlier this year, markets were pricing interest rate cuts by the Federal Reserve. As oil prices rallied above $100 a barrel, expectations shifted to a series of hikes.

To navigate the volatility, Gallo is using short duration to protect capital from sharp rate increases. He is also positioning for a flattening yield curve, in a bet that short-term yields will rise faster than long-term ones following Fed rate-hike signals.
Gallo also points to Japan as an important driver of the recent spike in Treasury yields. Local yields there have been rising, likely denting global demand for U.S. government bonds, he said

"Japan for decades had been sort of an underpinning of lower developed market sovereign yields around the world because capital was leaving Japan and seeking investment elsewhere," a trend now set to lose steam, he said.
He sees agency mortgage-backed securities as an attractive opportunity once rate volatility subsides, as they offer higher yields than Treasurys.

Gallo argues that once interest rates settle at current high levels, mortgage owners will have less incentive to refinance and prepay their lower-rate loans, reducing a source of instability for MBSs.

"Mortgage-backed securities tend to underperform when interest rates rise sharply or fall sharply...as a result, they get cheaper," Gallo said. "Once you expect some stability, then mortgages have a real opportunity to outperform."
